title: Don't Just Paste What AI Gives You
summary: In episode 1033 of the SuperDataScience podcast, @JonKrohnLearns discusses with Dr. Kate Niederhoffer, Chief Scientist at BetterUp, why you do not have to be a "meat proxy" for AI. She urges users not to paste in whatever the machine produces, but to iterate, stay in control of the inputs and the output, and use AI in a relational way. Sharing how you use it builds common ground and makes it feel safe for others to do the same.

title: What Most People Get Wrong About Evolution | Akarsh Kumar
summary: A lot of people in AI treat evolution as a dumb fallback, basically random search for when you can't take a gradient. Akarsh Kumar thinks that is wrong. Selection hangs on to partial solutions, so mutations only need to be useful about 1% of the time for the search to keep making progress. Akarsh is a PhD student at MIT working with Phillip Isola, works with Sakana AI, and is first author of the Fractured Entangled Representation paper with Kenneth Stanley, Jeff Clune and Joel Lehman. He tells Tim Scarfe why the path a learner takes may shape the structure of what it learns, and why that is a different way of looking at intelligence from the statistical one. Most of the conversation is about ASAL, the method he led for searching whole spaces of artificial worlds. Rather than predict what a rule will do, ASAL runs the simulation and asks a foundation model what happened. Mapped across all 262,144 Life-like rules, the most interesting worlds sit on one small island. Along the way: Game of Life, Lenia (with a clip from its creator, Bert Chan), neural cellular automata, Boids, Particle Life and the emergence of persistence. The last stretch is Core War, a programming game from the 1980s. Asked cold, LLMs write poor Redcode. Used as the mutation step in an evolutionary loop with a verifier, they produced warriors that, between them, beat or tied 96% of 294 human-written ones. Over repeated rounds the warriors trended towards generalists. --- TIMESTAMPS: 00:00:00 Intro: artificial life, ASAL and Core War in four minutes 00:04:19 Life as it could be, not just as it is A lot of people in AI treat evolution as a dumb fallback, basically random search for when you can't take a gradient. Akarsh Kumar thinks that is wrong. Selection hangs on to partial solutions, so mutations only need to be useful about 1% of the time for the search to keep making progress.

Akarsh is a PhD student at MIT working with Phillip Isola, works with Sakana AI, and is first author of the Fractured Entangled Representation paper with Kenneth Stanley, Jeff Clune and Joel Lehman. He tells Tim Scarfe why the path a learner takes may shape the structure of what it learns, and why that is a different way of looking at intelligence from the statistical one.

Most of the conversation is about ASAL, the method he led for searching whole spaces of artificial worlds. Rather than predict what a rule will do, ASAL runs the simulation and asks a foundation model what happened. Mapped across all 262,144 Life-like rules, the most interesting worlds sit on one small island. Along the way: Game of Life, Lenia (with a clip from its creator, Bert Chan), neural cellular automata, Boids, Particle Life and the emergence of persistence.

The last stretch is Core War, a programming game from the 1980s. Asked cold, LLMs write poor Redcode. Used as the mutation step in an evolutionary loop with a verifier, they produced warriors that, between them, beat or tied 96% of 294 human-written ones. Over repeated rounds the warriors trended towards generalists.

title: How to Connect Etsy and Printify to Claude or ChatGPT (Playground Sandbox Setup)
summary: Set up Playground Sandbox step by step: connect your Etsy shop and Printify account to Claude or ChatGPT so you can research, design and list print on demand products from one chat. This tutorial covers both the Claude setup and the ChatGPT setup, then runs a first prompt. Written version of every step: https://playgroundai.com/blog/how-to-connect-playground-to-claude-or-chatgpt#connect-playground-to-chatgpt Open Sandbox: https://playgroundai.com WHAT YOU NEED - A Playground account (this is the connection hub and your design tool) - A Printify account - An Etsy shop - Claude or ChatGPT (pick one and stick with it) STEP 1: CONNECT ETSY Log in to Etsy. At playgroundai.com open Sandbox, then Connectors, and click Connect next to Etsy. STEP 2: CONNECT PRINTIFY Click Connect next to Printify. In a new tab go to printify.com/app/account/api, click Generate, name the token (for example "Playground Connection"), keep all scopes and generate it. Copy the token, paste it into Playground and click Connect. Treat the token like a password and don't share it. STEP 3 FOR CLAUDE Copy the MCP server URL from the Connectors page. In Claude open Settings, then Connectors, then Add custom connector. Name it Playground, paste the URL, click Add, then Connect, and log in to Playground. STEP 3 FOR CHATGPT Copy the MCP server URL from the Connectors page. In ChatGPT open Settings, then Plugins, then Browse plugins. Click the plus sign to create a plugin, paste the URL and wait for the confirmation. STEP 4: YOUR FIRST PROMPT "Create three new designs in Playground for the homeschool mom niche. Pull from the templates I have favorited in Playground." Your designs appear on your Board in Playground as they're made. Set up Playground Sandbox step by step: connect your Etsy shop and Printify account to Claude or ChatGPT so you can research, design and list print on demand products from one chat. This tutorial covers both the Claude setup and the ChatGPT setup, then runs a first prompt.

Written version of every step: https://playgroundai.com/blog/how-to-connect-playground-to-claude-or-chatgpt#connect-playground-to-chatgpt
Open Sandbox: https://playgroundai.com

WHAT YOU NEED
- A Playground account (this is the connection hub and your design tool)
- A Printify account
- An Etsy shop
- Claude or ChatGPT (pick one and stick with it)

STEP 1: CONNECT ETSY
Log in to Etsy. At playgroundai.com open Sandbox, then Connectors, and click Connect next to Etsy.

STEP 2: CONNECT PRINTIFY
Click Connect next to Printify. In a new tab go to printify.com/app/account/api, click Generate, name the token (for example "Playground Connection"), keep all scopes and generate it. Copy the token, paste it into Playground and click Connect. Treat the token like a password and don't share it.

STEP 3 FOR CLAUDE
Copy the MCP server URL from the Connectors page. In Claude open Settings, then Connectors, then Add custom connector. Name it Playground, paste the URL, click Add, then Connect, and log in to Playground.

STEP 3 FOR CHATGPT
Copy the MCP server URL from the Connectors page. In ChatGPT open Settings, then Plugins, then Browse plugins. Click the plus sign to create a plugin, paste the URL and wait for the confirmation.

STEP 4: YOUR FIRST PROMPT
"Create three new designs in Playground for the homeschool mom niche. Pull from the templates I have favorited in Playground."
Your designs appear on your Board in Playground as they're made.

title: How MasterClass Builds Multi-Agent AI That Learners Can Trust
summary: Students perform better when given more personalized opportunities to learn. But scaling personalized learning has always proven to be challenging. Teachers are limited, students are many, time is finite – until now. AI agents are the first technology that give us a shot at shifting this equation in favor of the learner. MasterClass will share how AI now runs through our learning products, and how we made a multi-agent system reliable enough to put in front of real learners. The talk covers our observability stack on CoreWeave: full tracing of every agent step, an MCP server that exposes those traces back to agents, and the AgentOps loop that lets our system diagnose and improve itself. Where AI sits across MasterClass products today, and the bet behind going multi-agent Why learning raises the reliability bar — the failure modes that matter most when a learner is on the other end Tracing on CoreWeave: end-to-end visibility into multi-agent runs, and the failure taxonomy that emerged AgentOps in practice — agents querying traces via MCP to root-cause, cluster, and build datasets from real usage

title: Beyond Faster Simulation: Hitting NASA's 2030 CFD Benchmark and the Infrastructure for Physics AI
summary: AI has drastically reduced the cost of producing software code, transforming early prototypes into inexpensive "price checks" rather than lengthy debates. However, engineering teams are still limited by the high cost of simulations and the fragility of geometry workflows in hardware. In 2015, NASA’s CFD Vision 2030 study issued a significant challenge: enabling a single engineer to run and interpret 10,000 simulations in 24 hours without manual intervention. This turns out to be a dual challenge: 1) harnessing enough computing power at a reasonable cost, and 2) generating CAD boundaries and body-fitting meshing that does not break under parametric variation or require human intervention. In this talk, we will explain how nTop and CoreWeave surpassed NASA’s 2030 milestone four years ahead of schedule. They completed 10,000 Large Eddy Simulation (LES) CFD runs in just 32.2 hours. This was done across a drone platform design space comprising 2,400 variants. By combining nTop’s robust implicit geometry engine with a GPU-native Lattice Boltzmann (LBM) solver, we eliminated geometry failures and meshing steps entirely. A single engineer deployed a lights-out pipeline running across 280 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs on CoreWeave that sustained near 100% compute utilization without any interventions during the run. Finally, we will demonstrate how generating 14 TB of structured 3D flow data can transform CFD from a late-stage validation tool into the primary training engine for real-time physics AI surrogates operating in implicit latent space.

In this video I explain the idea, then build a working software factory with Claude Code running in Upstash Box sandboxes and point it at a real repo with 10 GitHub issues. It finished in 4 min 34 s, opened 9 pull requests, skipped the one vague issue, and all 9 fixes passed hidden tests the agents never saw. What you'll learn: - The core loop behind every software factory: issue → agent → independent check → human merge - Why running coding agents in parallel breaks, and the five fixes (sandbox per agent, claim labels, separate verifier + reviewer, live docs, human merges) - How Upstash Box gives each agent its own cloud sandbox: fast boot, snapshots, isolation, pause/resume, egress allowlists - A four-stage pipeline (triage, worker, verifier, reviewer) with typed handoffs between boxes - Grounding agents with Context7 live docs, with the API key injected outside the box - Why 7 of 9 verified PRs still conflicted, and the integrator stage that merged them - What it actually cost: $3.67 for the run, $6.37 for the integrator, about $0.01 of Box compute Links: - Factory code: https://github.com/PromtEngineer/software-factory - Upstash Box docs: https://upstash.com?utm_source=prompt1 - Context7: https://context7.com - Context7 Search (Upstash blog): https://upstash.com/blog/context7-search #softwarefactory #claudecode #aiagents #upstash

title: Why Microsoft Shut Down Its Undersea Data Centers

title: Systems of Record, Content & Intelligence: Where AI Fits in Enterprise Architecture
summary: Before you can talk about where AI adds value, you need to know which layer of the enterprise you are talking about. Terms covered: - System of Record: the authoritative source of truth for a data type. CRM for customers, ERP for financials, HR systems for employees. - System of Content: where unstructured content lives. Documents, emails, reports, contracts. Valuable, but harder to query and act on. - System of Intelligence: the AI and analytics layer sitting on top of both. It does not store data, it makes data useful. - AI Maturity: a framework for assessing how developed each layer is, and how effectively AI is applied across the organization Most organizations do not have all three working well at once. Knowing where an organization sits is what makes the AI conversation meaningful. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #EnterpriseAI #AIMaturity #DataStrategy #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Before you can talk about where AI adds value, you need to know which layer of the enterprise you are talking about.

Terms covered:
- System of Record: the authoritative source of truth for a data type. CRM for customers, ERP for financials, HR systems for employees.
- System of Content: where unstructured content lives. Documents, emails, reports, contracts. Valuable, but harder to query and act on.
- System of Intelligence: the AI and analytics layer sitting on top of both. It does not store data, it makes data useful.
- AI Maturity: a framework for assessing how developed each layer is, and how effectively AI is applied across the organization

Most organizations do not have all three working well at once. Knowing where an organization sits is what makes the AI conversation meaningful.

title: Quota Isn't Enough: Topology Aware Scheduling on Modern GPU Clusters
summary: Rack-scale systems are here! Fragmentation is widening the gap between “I have GPU quota” and “my job is actually running.” NVLink domains, rack boundaries, and the physical layout of the data center now shape whether a large training job can start, where it lands, and how efficiently it runs. On modern GPU clusters, quota is no longer enough. Topology has become a scheduling requirement. Kueue’s Topology Aware Scheduling (TAS) brings that reality into Kubernetes. In this session, you’ll learn how TAS works and the configuration choices that matter, including preferred versus required topologies and PodSet slices. You’ll also discover how topology-aware placement affects workload performance. Finally, you’ll walk away with the production lessons that do not show up in the happy path: sticky scheduling, quota debugging, fragmentation, and node hot swaps. Join us to understand how topology-aware scheduling helps AI teams turn expensive GPU capacity into actual training progress.

title: How Standard Kernel uses compound AI systems to optimize code and extract maximum GPU performance
summary: Standard Kernel uses compound AI systems to optimize code and extract maximum performance from GPUs. Our products help companies quickly transition their workloads to faster, higher-throughput, and more cost-effective setups across a variety of hardware options. We’ll also walk through case studies where we produced 11x faster world models and 7x faster options pricing models in just a few days.

title: Beyond the Benchmark: How Parallel Web Systems Builds Reliable Web Agents
summary: Building a capable web agent is only half the challenge; the harder problem is knowing whether it is working well in production. This talk explores how Parallel Web Systems measures quality across customer-specific use cases, monitors agent behavior, and automatically triages failures at scale. We’ll also discuss how we evaluate complex research tasks where correctness is nuanced, outputs are subjective, and traditional benchmarks fail to capture what customers actually value.

title: How Cline Embraces an Open-Weights Model Ecosystem for AI Agents
summary: Model capability alone doesn't make a reliable coding agent. The agent harness is what turns raw model performance into dependable, autonomous behavior. title: Data Architecture for AI: From Training Pipelines to Agent Memory
summary: Training, inference, RAG, and AI agents all consume data differently. Yet many organizations try to run them on infrastructure optimized for only one of those workloads, leading to performance bottlenecks, operational complexity, and unnecessary data movement. In this session, attendees will learn how data access patterns evolve across the AI lifecycle - from file and object storage for training, to KV cache for inference, to vector search, retrieval, and persistent memory for agents - and how to architect infrastructure that supports them within a unified platform. Drawing on deployments supporting large-scale AI environments, we will present a practical framework for matching storage, metadata, and memory architectures to specific AI workloads.

title: Inside a Game Where AI Agents Never Sleep
summary: What happens to an MMORPG when half the players never log off? Issac Lee, who runs AI and blockchain experiments at NEXUS, has been testing that idea. His team is filling game worlds with agent players instead of scripted NPCs, so a new title feels alive from day one. We get into why agent-generated content could be the next step after studio-made and user-generated games. We also cover how agent populations might solve the chicken-and-egg problem every multiplayer launch faces, and what it means when your fellow players are relentless and never need sleep. Isaac walks through the NEXUS lab: a text-to-3D world builder for Roblox, an AI pipeline that turns ONE store novels into short web dramas, a loop-based tool for natural pixel animation, and Da Vinci, the internal multi-agent framework the team uses to ship. Then the conversation turns to infrastructure. We talk about why NEXUS went from 200 hand-defined agent roles to a much thinner harness, whether custom harnesses still matter now that Claude and Codex exist, and why the Kimi release pushed the company to start building its own small data center for inference. We close on context: how much of your life you should hand to an AI, what personalized meeting notes could look like, and why shopping agents may force every ecommerce site to rethink who it's designing for. title: Training Your Own Embedding Model Is Not As Hard As You Think
summary: Fine-tune Embedding Gemma 2 (EmbeddingGemma 2) on your own data with Unsloth and LoRA in a free Colab notebook. I show how fine-tuning an embedding model differs from fine-tuning an LLM, then train Google's multimodal embedding model on two tasks: environmental sounds (ESC-50 top-1 24.5% to 65.8%) and search over my own YouTube transcripts (66.3% to 75.0% top-1 on videos it never saw), and check what it costs the rest of the model. You'll learn how to build question-passage training pairs, why in-batch negatives (MultipleNegativesRankingLoss) need a no-duplicates sampler, why training and search prompts must match, how LoRA works on a shared multimodal backbone, how to evaluate on unseen data, and a reload bug that silently breaks audio adapters. If you have fine-tuned embedding models for your own applications, share what worked for you in the comments. title: Rapidly Deploying Useful General-Purpose Robots at Walden Robotics
summary: Most Physical AI companies aim to build perfect autonomy before deploying. At Walden, we optimize for deployment first. Our general-purpose robots are doing useful work in production today, thanks to a full-stack approach that echoes what worked in autonomous driving and builds on recent breakthroughs in Large Behavior Models (LBMs). I'll cover how we scale that loop efficiently, and some of the open challenges.

title: Training Cognition SWE-1.7: Asynchronous RL at Global Scale
summary: This talk covers the systems and algorithmic challenges behind making globally distributed RL work at scale. We will discuss how we decouple training from inference, propagate compressed weight updates across datacenters, control policy staleness, and design the infrastructure to tolerate frequent hardware failures. We will also examine the training–inference mismatches that emerge in asynchronous RL and the techniques we use to preserve policy entropy and maintain stable learning over long training runs.

title: Claude Haiku 5.5: Anthropic's New Workhorse.
summary: Anthropic just released Claude Haiku 5.5, which it calls its cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model yet. For prompts under 100,000 tokens, it costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. That's 90% less than Haiku 4.5 and the same price as OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna. Above 100K tokens it's half off, and Anthropic estimates typical workloads cost about 75% less. On OSWorld 2.1, a computer-use benchmark, Anthropic reports 72.4%, up from 15.7% for Haiku 4.5. It's also the first Haiku with an adjustable effort setting. Anthropic positions it as a workhorse for summaries, classification, and subagent jobs alongside Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, and says the bigger models are still the better choice for complex agentic coding. All benchmark numbers are Anthropic's own; independent results aren't in yet. Also announced: Sonnet 5.5 cache reads are now half price. Max and Team plans get monthly API credits, rolling out this week: $100 on Max 5x, $200 on Max 20x, and up to $500 pooled on Team. Available today on the Claude API, AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure as claude-haiku-5-5. title: From World Models to Working Machines: Physical AI in the Real World

title: Fueling Innovation at Scale: Inside Pinterest’s Machine Learning Platform
summary: You'll leave this session knowing what mature model lifecycle management actually looks like, and what it takes to get there. title: Building the Voice OS at Willow
summary: What does it take to build voice AI that hundreds of thousands of people can use across their everyday applications? Accurate speech recognition is only the beginning, with the real challenge making the output fast, reliable, and personalized. In this session, Lawrence, Co-Founder and CTO of Willow Voice, shares the engineering and product lessons behind building voice AI at scale spanning supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and personalization. The session then examines personalization in-depth: establishing good defaults, learning from user corrections, and turning subjective writing preferences into behaviors a model can follow. Attendees will leave with lessons applicable to building specialized AI products well beyond voice.

title: Introducing OpenDocRouter: Call any OCR model in a single line of code

Replace in Document swaps the explanation into the Quill editor, turning the tool into a rephraser with document export. title: Prompt Regression Tester
summary: Compares a trusted prompt with a proposed change over the same test suite, three runs per case, and calls a regression only when the baseline holds and the candidate keeps failing. By Benjamin Nweke Project page: https://towardsdatascience.com/shipai/projects/prompt-regression-tester ShipAI is a Towards Data Science project. You can learn more about it here: https://towardsdatascience.com/shipai/about Key takeaways. 1. Each case runs three times per prompt, so a regression means a stable baseline pass and a stable candidate fail. 2. Hard checks guard dates, numbers and review states; an LLM judge with a rubric scores meaning, and disagreements stay visible. 3. On an EvidenceDesk suite, a candidate that swapped dates for “earlier” and “later” failed the versioned case 3 of 3. title: Autonomous MCP Agent
summary: An agent that finds open-source MCP servers on GitHub at run time, runs them in throwaway uvx environments, and replans when a tool fails. By Partha Sarkar Project page: https://towardsdatascience.com/shipai/projects/auto-mcp ShipAI is a Towards Data Science project. A planner splits the task, a discovery agent finds MCP servers on GitHub, and uvx runs each in isolation. 2. When the SQLite insert failed on a missing table, the LangGraph supervisor replanned: create the table first, then retry. 3. Three finance servers failed the stock briefing; a whitelisted yfinance-mcp fixed it, and working tools get reused for later steps. title: Mistral Large 4 aka "le Chonk": Europe's Biggest Open Model
summary: Mistral just announced Mistral Large 4, officially nicknamed "le Chonk." It's a mixture-of-experts model with about 1 trillion total parameters and around 50 billion active per token. It takes text and images and has a 1 million token context window. Mistral says it's a frontier-level open-weight model: competitive with the strongest open models in the world, and well ahead of any open model built in the US or Europe, especially on coding agents, cybersecurity, finance, and law. All benchmark numbers here are Mistral's own; independent results aren't in yet. Right now it's a preview API. Mistral says the open weights land at the end of October. Sources: Mistral announcement: https://mistral.ai/news/mistral-large-4/ Model docs: https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-large-4-0 CNBC: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/06/mistral-ai-model-le-chonk.html #MistralAI #MistralLarge4 #OpenSourceAI #LLM #AI #shorts

Right now it's a preview API. Mistral says the open weights land at the end of October.

title: Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM simulate 12,635-atom protein complex
summary: It can take more than a decade for a medical discovery to become a drug doctors can prescribe. Researchers from @Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN and IBM are exploring how hybrid quantum-classical workflows could help accelerate this timeline–with exciting results. Earlier this year, the collaboration successfully simulated the chemistry of two protein complexes with binding agents, T4-Lysozyme and Trypsin. The largest simulation of a Trypsin complex reached 12,635 atoms and more than 30,000 orbitals, earning the milestone of largest heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) electronic-structure calculation to date: https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/cleveland-clinic-riken-chemistry Recently nominated as a 2026 Gordon Bell finalist (https://www.ibm.com/quantum/blog/gordon-bell-finalists-2026), the work showed an improvement in accuracy by 210x within a key step of the workflow over previous approaches, attained through new algorithm developments and the close integration of QPUs, CPUs and GPUs. In the latest entry of our research spotlight series, Dr. Kennie Merz. and Dr. Lara Jehi from Cleveland Clinic join IBM Quantum Head of Applied Quantum Science - Sarah Sheldon to explain how this deep integration of computing paradigms, known as quantum-centric supercomputing, helped achieve this remarkable moment in chemistry simulation at scale.

title: Workslop Costs a 10K Firm $9M a Year (with Jeff Hancock and Kate Niederhoffer)

title: Jev AI vs Open Source: Can GLiNER Replace It?
summary: Jev is one of the most hyped AI models of the year, and it isn't an LLM. TypeSafe's "System One" model doesn't generate text. It makes typed, calibrated decisions in ~90ms. In this video we cover what Jev is and how its API works. We look at why calibrated probability is the real unlock, where Jev fits next to LLMs (and where it doesn't), and the open-source "OpenJev" alternatives you can run on your own machine. Finally, we think fast and slow, pairing a System One model with an LLM coach to beat solo Jev at Doom. 📌 Full article with benchmarks, charts and methodology: https://jamesbriggs.io/understanding-jev What we found: - Calibration: Jev's confidence means something. ECE 0.053 vs 0.119 for gpt-5.6-luna on CLINC150. - Speed: ~90ms per call on the server vs ~700ms for gpt-5.6-luna with no reasoning. Extra questions in the same call add no latency. - Accuracy: Jev matches or beats gpt-5.6-luna on 5 of 6 intent, tool-selection and guardrail benchmarks. - Open source: GLiNER2.5 and GLiGuard run in 10–50ms on an M4 Pro Mac and come close on several benchmarks. They don't match Jev's calibration yet. - Fast + slow: adding an LLM coach to Jev and GLiNER gives ~4x their solo Doom deathmatch scores. ⏱️ Chapters 0:00 Intro 1:22 What is JEV? 2:40 Inputs and outputs 4:26 Three types of decision 6:35 Calibrated probability 10:38 Ultra-fast 11:44 Where JEV fits 14:58 Closed source 16:39 Open-source alternatives 20:28 GLiNER 23:33 The trade-offs 25:42 Thinking fast and slow 31:30 What to make of JEV 👋 Find me X: https://x.com/jamescalam LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jamescalam/ GitHub: https://github.com/jamescalam #AI #LLM #AIAgents
summary_html:
Jev is one of the most hyped AI models of the year, and it isn't an LLM. TypeSafe's "System One" model doesn't generate text. It makes typed, calibrated decisions in ~90ms.

In this video we cover what Jev is and how its API works. We look at why calibrated probability is the real unlock, where Jev fits next to LLMs (and where it doesn't), and the open-source "OpenJev" alternatives you can run on your own machine. Finally, we think fast and slow, pairing a System One model with an LLM coach to beat solo Jev at Doom.

📌 Full article with benchmarks, charts and methodology:
https://jamesbriggs.io/understanding-jev

What we found:
- Calibration: Jev's confidence means something. ECE 0.053 vs 0.119 for gpt-5.6-luna on CLINC150.
- Speed: ~90ms per call on the server vs ~700ms for gpt-5.6-luna with no reasoning. Extra questions in the same call add no latency.
- Accuracy: Jev matches or beats gpt-5.6-luna on 5 of 6 intent, tool-selection and guardrail benchmarks.
- Open source: GLiNER2.5 and GLiGuard run in 10–50ms on an M4 Pro Mac and come close on several benchmarks. They don't match Jev's calibration yet.
- Fast + slow: adding an LLM coach to Jev and GLiNER gives ~4x their solo Doom deathmatch scores.

title: CoreWeave Forge: Demo from Fully Connected 2026, with Corey Sanders
summary: The complete CoreWeave Forge demo from Fully Connected 2026: Corey Sanders takes a help desk agent through the whole AI loop, uncut. Start building on CoreWeave Forge: https://www.coreweave.com/forge What you're watching: Corey's IT help desk agent files tickets, sets a priority, and routes them, and sometimes it gets the priority or the routing wrong. Over eleven minutes he fixes it without leaving Forge: he instruments the app, finds the failing pattern in production, picks a fix with ARIA, trains with serverless reinforcement learning, proves the new version wins, and ships it with its history attached. Chapters 0:00 The help desk app, and the problem 0:53 Signing in to Forge; ARIA prepares the Agent Lens diff 2:30 Observe: Agent Lens traces, costs, tools, and spans 3:38 Curate: tags and an LLM judge 4:46 Insights finds the pattern: 1.6% of conversations misprioritized 5:26 Improve: ARIA's performance summary 6:32 Would serverless RL work here? 7:14 RL runs in Weights & Biases Models 8:08 Scaling the runs in CoreWeave Sandboxes 8:29 ARIA's report picks the best run 9:01 Evaluate: new model against old, on his own traces 10:14 Lineage: where the new model came from 10:37 Run, observe, curate, improve, evaluate, and run again 11:04 Sign up for CoreWeave Forge The tools in the demo: CoreWeave Agent Lens records every step the agent takes in production and groups the conversations that fail the same way, so you start with the cases that matter. ARIA, our AI Research & Iteration Agent, reads your runs and traces and answers with a plan, from the code change that adds observability to what to try next. title: Grounded Generation, Hallucinations & LLM Evaluation: Assessing Model Output Quality
summary: AI can be confidently wrong. Here is why it happens, how grounding fixes it, and how to measure whether it worked. Terms covered: - Hallucination: models are trained to generate statistically likely text, not to verify facts. When a model does not know, it fills the gap with something plausible. - Grounded Generation: anchoring responses in verified, retrieved sources so answers are traceable and far less likely to be fabricated - LLM Evaluation: assessing outputs for accuracy, relevance, coherence, cost and safety, as an ongoing practice rather than a one-time check - RAG Evaluation: measuring retrieval and generation separately, because a system can retrieve well and generate poorly, or generate fluently from the wrong sources The goal is not perfect AI. It is trustworthy AI, and that requires knowing how to measure it. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #LLM #Hallucinations #ResponsibleAI #AIGlossary #H2Oai

title: How a Logistics Giant Keeps AI Data Locked Down
summary: Picture a startup with ten engineers hammering away on AI and one person lying awake over a $20,000 bill that hasn't arrived yet. That's the scenario we put to Jason Ward, who handles FinOps for AI at C.H. Robinson and recently joined the FinOps Foundation's AI working group. Jason's first answer is not glamorous: tag every AI resource so you know who owns it. The rest of the episode is what that makes possible. He walks through how C.H. Robinson runs AI across order entry, quoting, booking, and tracking, and why the team routes Anthropic models through Vertex AI to keep data locked down. Then come the metrics. Jason uses AI to dig through his own observability platform for signals he didn't know were there. One of them is how chatty a model is. That signal turned a prompt bloat alert into a bug in the code that kept retrying and burning tokens. Its opposite, context starvation, burns tokens too: a model with too little context keeps failing and trying again. We also cover why agentic and conversational workloads need separate baselines. Jason explains why cost per order is the easy win, and why most of the real work doesn't fit into neat discrete tasks. That's where his experimental cost per thought metric comes in, with reasoning ratio and cache hit rate alongside it. His advice is simple: your AI is the best tool you have for understanding your AI. title: Stanford Univ: New AI Attention: SwiLA
summary: Softmax attention’s KV-cache is a dead end for infinite (or extreme large) context, but standard Linear Attention fundamentally destroys associative recall (Mamba, DeltaNet). So how do we get the best of both worlds? Meet SwiLA (Switching Linear Attention) by Stanford Univ. Switching Linear Attention completely eliminates the transformer's massive memory cache without sacrificing associative recall by modeling sequence routing as online expectation-maximization over a mixture of linear regressors. Dive into the math of how this non-linear recurrence dynamically routes context to constant-size memory experts, finally fixing the critical flaw of sub-quadratic language models. summary: In episode 1032 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Michael Andrew, CDO at Salesforce how Salesforce tackled its internal data chaos, including duplicate records and disparate systems, leading to the development and deployment of their Data 360 product. title: How Many Iterations Does a Good Spec Need?
summary: A strong specification rarely emerges fully formed. It improves through focused iteration—clarifying assumptions, resolving ambiguity, testing edge cases, and aligning the intended outcome with real constraints. Hari Krishnan, author of Spec-Driven Development, explains how teams can refine a specification and why there’s no universal number of iterations. The goal isn’t perfection—it’s reaching the point where developers and AI coding agents have enough shared context to implement the right solution confidently. Learn more about Spec-Driven Development: https://hubs.la/Q04ypXVz0 #SpecDrivenDevelopment #AICoding #ContextEngineering #SoftwareDevelopment #CodingAgents #Shorts

title: SLMs, Fine-Tuning & LLMOps: Building Production-Ready Language Models
summary: Not every use case needs a large model. Smaller and purpose-built is often faster, cheaper and better suited to the job. Terms covered: - SLM (Small Language Model): fewer parameters, trading breadth for precision. Runs on-premises or on edge devices with no cloud dependency. - SLM Development: designing, training and optimizing a small model for a well-defined task or dataset - Fine-Tuning Engine: taking a pre-trained model and training it further on domain-specific data, so it learns the language of law, medicine or your business - LLMOps: the infrastructure and practices for deploying, managing, monitoring and updating language models over time A hospital running clinical documentation on local servers. A manufacturer processing quality reports on factory floor devices. Terms covered:
- SLM (Small Language Model): fewer parameters, trading breadth for precision. Runs on-premises or on edge devices with no cloud dependency.

- Fine-Tuning Engine: taking a pre-trained model and training it further on domain-specific data, so it learns the language of law, medicine or your business
- LLMOps: the infrastructure and practices for deploying, managing, monitoring and updating language models over time

title: How a Voice Agent Learns the Rhythm of Conversation — Shawn Wen
summary: Tsung-Hsien (Shawn) Wen, CTO of PolyAI, tells Tim Scarfe why voice agents are harder than text agents. Voice adds time, and a good conversation depends on adapting to the person on the line, not just on reasoning to the best answer. Shawn describes an audio-native model (Dialog-RSN-1) that first predicts a turn-taking signal, then replies in text with citations, and writes the transcript last so enterprises can audit it. Along the way: training on real, noisy calls with synthetic noise added, and why over-cleaned audio made the new model worse. Latency, and what a voice agent should do while it thinks. Why a voice with a hint of regional accent beats a generic one. Why public benchmarks fall short for voice, why enterprises want to own their agent harness, and whether behaviour belongs in the harness or in the weights. The last stretch is about working with agents: cognitive debt, the shift from producing content to checking it, Wispr Flow, building tools that agents can use, and whether slop is in the eye of the reader. Tsung-Hsien (Shawn) Wen, CTO of PolyAI, tells Tim Scarfe why voice agents are harder than text agents. Voice adds time, and a good conversation depends on adapting to the person on the line, not just on reasoning to the best answer. Shawn describes an audio-native model (Dialog-RSN-1) that first predicts a turn-taking signal, then replies in text with citations, and writes the transcript last so enterprises can audit it.

Along the way: training on real, noisy calls with synthetic noise added, and why over-cleaned audio made the new model worse. Latency, and what a voice agent should do while it thinks. Why a voice with a hint of regional accent beats a generic one. Why public benchmarks fall short for voice, why enterprises want to own their agent harness, and whether behaviour belongs in the harness or in the weights.

The last stretch is about working with agents: cognitive debt, the shift from producing content to checking it, Wispr Flow, building tools that agents can use, and whether slop is in the eye of the reader.

title: The Caveman Prompting Challenge
summary: Caveman prompting has one rule: why use many words when few do the trick? It saves tokens on the way in and on the way out. Push it too far, though, and the output falls apart. So how far is too far? Nobody has benchmarked it yet, and that question opens our conversation with James Barney, Head of Forward Labs at MetLife. James spends his days connecting new AI capabilities to old business problems across dozens of regulatory regimes, and he still finds time to push code. He explains how the FinOps Foundation's AI working group took on the most basic question: which model for which workload, and why the answer always comes down to cost, speed, and accuracy. We get into Anthropic's launch pricing for Fable, why a million tokens is easy to price and hard to explain, and why every stakeholder eventually tells you what they really care about once you name the wrong North Star. From there it gets practical. Start with the smartest model, then step down and add harness until quality holds. Treat exploration tokens like local builds and production tokens like pipelines. Govern agents the way you govern people, with proactive blocks, reactive checks, and policy as code an agent can actually read. We close on a bigger shift. When a chat window can pull from every dashboard at once, do we still need dashboards? James thinks mostly not, with one catch he calls the latent shopper problem: some insights only come from browsing data you did not know to ask about. summary_html:
Caveman prompting has one rule: why use many words when few do the trick? It saves tokens on the way in and on the way out. Push it too far, though, and the output falls apart. So how far is too far? Nobody has benchmarked it yet, and that question opens our conversation with James Barney, Head of Forward Labs at MetLife.

James spends his days connecting new AI capabilities to old business problems across dozens of regulatory regimes, and he still finds time to push code. He explains how the FinOps Foundation's AI working group took on the most basic question: which model for which workload, and why the answer always comes down to cost, speed, and accuracy. We get into Anthropic's launch pricing for Fable, why a million tokens is easy to price and hard to explain, and why every stakeholder eventually tells you what they really care about once you name the wrong North Star.

From there it gets practical. Start with the smartest model, then step down and add harness until quality holds. Treat exploration tokens like local builds and production tokens like pipelines. Govern agents the way you govern people, with proactive blocks, reactive checks, and policy as code an agent can actually read.

We close on a bigger shift. When a chat window can pull from every dashboard at once, do we still need dashboards? James thinks mostly not, with one catch he calls the latent shopper problem: some insights only come from browsing data you did not know to ask about.

title: Meet The Startup: Probabl: by the Creators of Scikit-Learn
summary: The creators of scikit-learn are GPU-accelerating machine learning — and partnering with NVIDIA to do it. Yann Lechelle, co-founder of Probabl, sat down with us to share why the team behind the world's most downloaded ML framework is doubling down on statistical machine learning — not generative AI — and what that means for the future of tabular data. Scikit-learn has surpassed 5 billion downloads, with 1.3 million GitHub projects depending on it. It's the backbone of data science as we know it. But it was built for CPUs — and the world has changed. Probabl is now offloading key algorithms to GPU, leveraging the Array API as an abstraction layer so that new generations of NVIDIA chips plug in seamlessly, without rewriting everything from scratch. Their new product, Skore, wraps scikit-learn and tabular large models into a unified ML platform — with the goal of becoming the world's leading tabular AI company within five years. And as Yann points out, it's not just data scientists using these tools anymore: agents are now the largest driver of scikit-learn downloads, consuming documentation and frameworks at machine speed. The partnership with NVIDIA Inception is about more than compute — it's about building the abstraction layer that maximizes intelligence per gigawatt, for humans and agents alike. Learn more about how NVIDIA Inception supports startups building the future of AI — and explore what GPU-accelerated ML can do for your workflows at nvidia.com/inception.

title: Gemini 4 Argon: The New Frontier
summary: Gemini 4 Argon can generate up to 1 million output tokens in a single response, up from 64K in earlier Gemini models. Most frontier models today cap a single response at around 128K. Arena's testing puts Argon on the Pareto frontier of performance vs. cost: 33% lower cost per task than GPT-6.1 Sol and 70% lower than Claude Opus 5.5. Argon isn't publicly available yet. It's rolling out first to trusted testers through Google's Fairwind program. Fun fact: argon is the third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere.
